title: IRGC Claims HIMARS Destruction at Ali Al Salem and FPS Radar at Ahmad Al Jaber. Kuwait Says 'Material Damage' to Border Posts.
narrative:
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps announced on July 12–13 that its Aerospace Force destroyed US HIMARS missile launchers at Ali Al Salem Air Base and a fixed phased-array radar system at Ahmad Al Jaber Air Base in Kuwait, describing the strikes as "the third phase of Operation Reciprocity." Fars News Agency reported that HIMARS launchers and accompanying missile pods, described as "ready to fire toward Iran," were destroyed in a "precision drone operation," citing unofficial reports of three US officers killed and several wounded. The IRGC also claimed destruction of fuel depots and Patriot air-defense systems at Ali Al Salem. Kuwait's government characterized the same events as "material damage" to three northern border posts and an offshore Kuwait Oil Company drilling platform, with one worker injured in a single drone strike. The Kuwaiti Foreign Ministry called Iran's attacks "a very dangerous escalation" but did not confirm or deny damage to any military facility.

Defence Security Asia published satellite imagery and video analysis showing ballistic-missile impact signatures at Ali Al Salem consistent with the IRGC's described targeting pattern — fuel-storage areas and air-defense positions. The imagery confirms physical damage to the base but cannot independently verify whether HIMARS systems, which are mobile and routinely relocated, were present at the moment of impact. The FPS radar at Ahmad Al Jaber is a high-value early-warning asset whose destruction would create a gap in Kuwait's air-surveillance coverage that cannot be quickly replaced, unlike mobile systems like HIMARS or Patriot which can be redeployed from other theaters.

CENTCOM has not issued a specific denial of the HIMARS or radar claims. The Pentagon's pattern since the July 9 Ali Al Salem ASR-1000 radar strike has been to issue generalized statements about "minimal impact" without addressing specific systems by name. The Air & Space Forces Magazine June 5 exclusive revealed that the Combined Air Operations Center at Al Udeid, Qatar was "severely damaged" and rendered inoperable — suggesting the Pentagon's "minimal impact" framing extends across multiple theaters. Kuwait hosts approximately 13,000 US military personnel. The HIMARS system, if confirmed present at Ali Al Salem, would be the first ground-based offensive missile system publicly acknowledged as deployed in Kuwait during the conflict — a significant escalation from the radar and air-defense assets previously known to be stationed there.
analysis:
The gap between IRGC's specific claims (HIMARS launchers, Patriot batteries, FPS radar, fuel depots, three officers killed) and Kuwait's vague "material damage" to border posts and a drilling platform is the widest attribution asymmetry in the conflict to date. Kuwait has acknowledged attacks on its territory while refusing to confirm the specific military targets Iran claims to have destroyed. This diplomatic posture serves both Washington — which avoids admitting offensive-capability losses — and Kuwait — which avoids being seen as a co-combatant. The IRGC's specificity (named bases, named systems, casualty figures) versus Kuwait's vagueness ("material damage," one injured worker) creates an information vacuum that only satellite imagery can fill.

The Ali Al Salem ASR-1000 radar was already confirmed destroyed by OSINT on July 9. The July 12–13 strikes appear to be follow-up attacks on the same base, targeting the systems the radar was protecting. If HIMARS launchers were present, their destruction means Iran has now struck both the sensor (radar) and the shooter (HIMARS) at the same base across two separate strike packages — a coordinated degrade-and-destroy sequence, not opportunistic targeting. The three-officer casualty claim is the element most likely to be either confirmed or denied by leaked reporting in the next 48 hours.

The broader structural pattern is the Pentagon's consistent refusal to address specific system losses by name. The ASR-1000 was confirmed destroyed by satellite, not by CENTCOM disclosure. The Al Udeid CAOC was revealed as inoperable by trade press, not by Pentagon announcement. If HIMARS and FPS radar losses are confirmed through the same OSINT channels, the gap between physical reality and official disclosure becomes the story itself — the US military's damage-disclosure posture has shifted from "we assess no significant damage" to silence, which is a different kind of admission.
verdict: [SIPHONED VERDICT]: The systematic pattern of Kuwait confirming attacks while refusing to confirm military targets — a diplomatic posture that serves both Washington and Kuwait — has now expanded from radar systems to offensive missile launchers and early-warning radar. The IRGC's specificity versus Kuwait's vagueness creates an information vacuum that only satellite imagery can fill, and the Pentagon's shift from "minimal impact" statements to silence on specific system losses is itself an evidentiary signal. If HIMARS launchers were present, the degrade-and-destroy sequence (radar July 9, launchers July 12–13) represents the first documented Iranian coordinated multi-package strike against the same base's sensor-shooter pair.
